name: Teduglutide (Gattex/Revestive)

b.x: Sixty-three percent response versus thirty percent on placebo. That single number from the STEPS trial (n=86) [1] carried teduglutide to FDA approval for short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure. Teduglutide (Gattex, Revestive; CAS 197922-42-2) is a 33-amino acid recombinant analog of glucagon-like peptide-2. A single substitution at position 2 (alanine to glycine) blocks dipeptidyl peptidase-IV cleavage; that one change extends the half-life from roughly 7 minutes to about 2 hours. Enough for once-daily subcutaneous dosing. The drug triggers intestinal mucosal growth by activating GLP-2 receptors on subepithelial myofibroblasts and enteric neurons. Villus height increases. Crypt depth increases. Absorptive surface area expands. The practical result: patients absorb more fluid and nutrients from the gut, so they can reduce or stop parenteral nutrition. Long-term data backs this up. STEPS-2 [2] and STEPS-3 [3] confirmed sustained parenteral support reductions over 30 months of continuous treatment. In pediatric patients aged 1 year and older, Wales and colleagues (n=85) [4] reported an 82.1% response rate at 96 weeks. Both adults and children receive the same weight-based dose: 0.05 mg/kg/day. The limitations are real. The STEPS trial enrolled only 86 patients. Cost runs $520,000 to $550,000 per year at list price. Colonoscopy surveillance is mandatory. And intestinal adaptation reverses within weeks of stopping, which means therapy is indefinite for most patients.

Native GLP-2 lasts about 7 minutes in circulation before dipeptidyl peptidase-IV chews it apart. Teduglutide puts glycine in place of alanine at position 2, and that single amino acid change blocks the enzyme's cleavage site. Half-life jumps to approximately 2 hours. Once injected subcutaneously (bioavailability around 88%, per Marier et al.) [5], teduglutide binds GLP-2 receptors on intestinal subepithelial myofibroblasts and enteric neurons. Receptor activation kicks off a trophic cascade: crypt cell proliferation accelerates, villus height and crypt depth increase, and new nutrient transporters appear on the mucosal surface. Mesenteric blood flow rises through nitric oxide-dependent vasodilation. Epithelial tight junctions tighten, improving barrier function. Teduglutide also slows gastric emptying and dials down gastric acid secretion. Both effects give the shortened bowel more time to absorb what passes through it. The net result is measurable. Plasma citrulline levels (a biomarker for enterocyte mass) start climbing within the first few weeks. By week 24 in the STEPS trial, 63% of patients on 0.05 mg/kg/day achieved at least a 20% reduction in weekly parenteral support volume. Peak plasma concentration hits between 3 and 5 hours post-injection, and the drug clears with a terminal half-life of roughly 2 hours (shorter in SBS patients, around 1.3 hours, likely due to altered distribution).
Teduglutide benefits center on restoring intestinal function and reducing dependence on intravenous nutrition in short bowel syndrome.

- The STEPS trial (n=86) [1] showed 63% of patients on 0.05 mg/kg/day achieved at least 20% reduction in weekly parenteral support volume at 24 weeks, compared with 30% on placebo (p=0.002). - Some patients reach complete enteral autonomy. Full independence from parenteral nutrition is the outcome SBS patients describe as life-changing in community reports. - Intestinal absorptive surface area physically increases through higher villus height, deeper crypts, and upregulated nutrient transporter expression. - Pediatric patients respond even better. Wales et al. (n=85) [4] found an 82.1% response rate at 96 weeks in children aged 1 year and older, with a mean parenteral fluid reduction of 30.1 mL/kg/day. - Quality of life improves in a way that's hard to quantify on paper. Fewer hours tethered to an IV pole means sleeping through the night, traveling, and returning to work. - Long-term durability is confirmed. STEPS-3 [3] showed sustained benefit at 30 months of continuous treatment with no signal of efficacy fade.

Highly positive among the small SBS patient community.

Life-changing reduction or elimination of TPN dependence is the dominant reported outcome. Main barriers are cost/insurance access and colonoscopy requirement, not tolerability. No off-label or performance community use documented.

Science & Community Aligned

SBS patients using teduglutide are the clinical trial population: there is no off-label community. Scientific evidence and patient community both report strong efficacy with TPN reduction as the primary outcome. Community concerns (cost, colonoscopy burden, abdominal side effects) are consistent with the clinical safety and access literature. No dose discrepancy exists: patients follow the FDA-approved 0.05 mg/kg/day weight-based dose.

Teduglutide is supplied as a 5 mg lyophilized vial in 30-vial kits. Reconstitute with the 0.5 mL sterile water for injection included in the kit. Do not use bacteriostatic water. Gently roll the vial; do not shake. Let it sit 30 seconds before drawing. That gives you a 10 mg/mL concentration. For a 70 kg patient at the standard 0.05 mg/kg/day dose, you need 3,500 mcg (3.5 mg), which is 0.35 mL or 35 units on a 100-unit insulin syringe. A 50 kg patient draws 25 units (2,500 mcg). A 100 kg patient needs 5,000 mcg (0.5 mL), but only 0.38 mL (3.8 mg) can be drawn from one vial (GATTEX label, section 2.6). At the standard dose, anyone over 76 kg needs more than 3.8 mg, so more than one vial; the prescriber says how many. The non-obvious thing beginners miss: you must use each reconstituted vial within 3 hours. There are no preservatives. Don't prepare vials ahead of time. Bedtime dosing is the community favorite because it helps you sleep through the early abdominal bloating instead of sitting with it all day. Rotate injection sites across four abdominal quadrants; mark the quadrant on the vial if it helps you track rotation.
Cycling Protocol

Teduglutide is used continuously as a chronic therapy. There is no cycling protocol: the drug is administered daily without breaks. Discontinuation leads to regression of intestinal adaptation within weeks. Regular colonoscopy surveillance and lipase/amylase monitoring every 6 months are required during ongoing therapy. Clinical reassessment of parenteral support needs should occur at least every 6 months.
Teduglutide (Gattex/Revestive) Cycle

Teduglutide is a chronic disease therapy, not a performance peptide. There is no receptor desensitization, hormonal axis suppression, or antibody formation rationale for cycling breaks at clinical doses. Intestinal mucosal adaptation is progressive and reverses within weeks of discontinuation: indefinite continuous therapy is required for maintained benefit.
No cycling indicators: therapy should continue indefinitely
Regression of intestinal adaptation (increased PS requirements) signals missed doses or inadequate therapy, not a cycling signal
Colonoscopy surveillance and biannual lipase/amylase are safety checkpoints, not cycling triggers

Works With
Somatropin (Zorbtive)

Zorbtive (somatropin for injection) is FDA-approved for SBS. Historical triple approach pre-teduglutide: GH + glutamine + optimized diet. Teduglutide largely supplanted GH/glutamine due to superior durability. Some clinicians use both targeting complementary mechanisms (systemic anabolic vs. direct intestinal mucosal trophic). No dedicated RCT for the teduglutide + Zorbtive combination.
Zorbtive: 0.1 mg/kg/day SC (max 8 mg/day) for 4 weeks alongside optimized diet; teduglutide continued indefinitely. Historical use, not standard of care.
L-Glutamine (Nutrestore oral supplementation)

Historically part of the pre-teduglutide SBS triple approach (GH + glutamine + optimized diet). FDA-approved oral glutamine (Nutrestore, 30g/day) used as adjunct. Some clinicians continue alongside teduglutide for additional enterocyte support; no RCT data for the teduglutide + glutamine combination. Not standard of care.
Avoid
Oral anticoagulants (warfarin)
Teduglutide increases intestinal absorption: enhanced warfarin absorption may significantly raise INR and bleeding risk. Monitor INR closely; dose adjustments likely needed.
Immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus)
Enhanced GI absorption may increase cyclosporine/tacrolimus levels and toxicity risk. Monitor drug levels closely when starting or adjusting teduglutide dose.

Gattex has no boxed warning. Its label lists five warnings and precautions instead (section 5), led by acceleration of neoplastic growth. Based on the drug's growth effect on gut tissue and on rodent tumor findings, the label says teduglutide may cause hyperplastic changes, including neoplasia. In 2-year studies, male rats developed more bile duct and jejunal adenomas, and mice more gallbladder papillary adenomas. Male mice on the highest dose also developed jejunal adenocarcinomas. In the adult trials, 14 patients had GI tract polyps found after starting treatment. Three men were diagnosed with cancer; two had long smoking histories and lung cancer. Adults need a colonoscopy and upper GI endoscopy within 6 months before the first dose, with any polyps removed. Both are repeated at the end of year 1. After that, it's at least every 5 years if no polyp turns up, or standard polyp follow-up if one does. Children get a fecal occult blood test before starting and every year after. New or unexplained blood in the stool triggers a colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy plus an upper GI endoscopy. A colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy also follows after 1 year, then every 5 years. A cancer of the GI tract, liver, gallbladder, bile ducts or pancreas means stopping teduglutide. For a cancer elsewhere, continuing is a benefit-risk call. For people already at higher cancer risk, the label says to use it only if the benefits outweigh the risks. Intestinal obstruction, the second warning, hit 3 of 77 patients (4%) on the label dose in the 24-week placebo-controlled trials, and none on placebo. Teduglutide is paused while a blockage is managed and can restart once it clears. Patients with a stoma had more stoma complications, 42% vs 14% on placebo. Third come gallbladder, bile duct and pancreas disease. Cholecystitis, cholangitis, gallstones and pancreatitis were all reported in trials. The label calls for bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, lipase and amylase within 6 months before starting, then at least every 6 months. Fluid overload is the fourth warning. As the gut absorbs more fluid, parenteral support may need to come down. In the placebo-controlled trials, fluid overload (edema included) hit 12% vs 7% on placebo, and 2 patients on teduglutide developed congestive heart failure. Stopping can swing the other way, into fluid and electrolyte imbalance, so those need checks after the last dose. The fifth warning covers oral drugs, since teduglutide can increase how much of them gets absorbed. One trial patient on the benzodiazepine prazepam fell into a coma in the first week; it resolved 5 days after both drugs stopped. Oral drugs that need titration or have a narrow therapeutic index call for monitoring, and their dose may need to drop. Common reactions come from the placebo-controlled trials, with 77 adults on the label dose. Abdominal pain led at 30% (22% on placebo), and nausea hit 23% (20%). Upper respiratory tract infection reached 21% (12%), while abdominal distension showed the widest gap, 20% vs 2%. Injection site reactions ran 13% (12% on placebo), vomiting 12% (10%), and hypersensitivity such as rash or itching 10% (7%). The label recommends rotating injection sites across the abdomen, thighs and upper arms. In 41 children aged 1 to under 17, the safety profile was similar to that in adults. In pregnancy, case reports haven't identified a drug-linked risk. Rat and rabbit studies found no embryo-fetal harm at up to 686 and 657 times human exposure. Breastfeeding isn't recommended during treatment; the label cites possible serious reactions in the infant, including tumorigenicity. Call the prescriber right away for abdominal pain or swelling, trouble passing stool or gas, vomiting, or a swollen or blocked stoma. The same goes for fever, chills, dark urine, yellowing skin or eyes, swollen ankles, fast weight gain or trouble breathing.

Fluid overload as absorption improves: common if PS volumes are not proactively reduced; use urine output increase (≥1 mL/kg/day above baseline) as trigger to reduce PS by 10–20%

No response at week 24 (<20% PS reduction): confirm injection technique and site rotation; verify compliance; check for concurrent infection or metabolic issue; colon-in-continuity patients have higher response rates: its absence may explain non-response

Teduglutide is FDA-approved (brand name Gattex in the US, Revestive in the EU) for adults and pediatric patients aged 1 year and older with short bowel syndrome associated with intestinal failure who require parenteral support. It carries full regulatory approval, not investigational or research-only status. FDA ended the Gattex REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) on Aug 26, 2026 (NDA 203441, supplement 28). FDA found the program no longer necessary for the benefits to outweigh the risks. The label warnings and colonoscopy monitoring still apply. There is no compounding pharmacy or grey-market version of teduglutide. The combination of prohibitive cost ($520,000 to $550,000/year at list price) and mandatory colonoscopy surveillance has prevented any research-chemical market from forming. WADA status is not relevant, as teduglutide has no performance-improving application. This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Teduglutide should only be used under the supervision of a qualified healthcare provider experienced in managing short bowel syndrome.

protocols.goal: Short Bowel Syndrome with intestinal failure: pediatric (≥1 year)

phases.name: Pediatric Initiation and Maintenance
phases.notes: FDA approved November 2019 for pediatric patients ≥1 year. Wales et al. 2024 (n=85, PMID 38873891): 82.1% response rate at week 96; mean PS fluid reduction 30.1 mL/kg/day. Favorable predictors: colon in continuity, longer teduglutide exposure, greater remaining small intestine. Pediatric-specific surveillance: fecal occult blood test pre-treatment; colonoscopy at 1 year (not required pre-treatment for children per pediatric label). Calculated dose volumes will be very small: use appropriate pediatric syringe for accuracy.

protocols.duration: Indefinite: ongoing as long as clinical benefit continues
protocols.monitoringNotes: Fecal occult blood test pre-treatment. Colonoscopy at 1 year post-initiation. Lipase/amylase every 6 months. Monitor growth parameters and nutritional markers. Reassess PS requirements every 6 months.

faqs.q: Why do all three dosing tiers show the same dose?
faqs.a: Teduglutide has one approved dose, 0.05 mg/kg (50 mcg/kg) once daily, and every tier shows it. Short bowel syndrome patients get the same per-kg dose whatever the severity. Your daily amount scales with body weight: about 2,500 mcg at 50 kg, 3,500 mcg at 70 kg and 5,000 mcg at 100 kg.

faqs.q: How soon can parenteral nutrition be reduced after starting teduglutide?
faqs.a: First reductions in parenteral support volume (10-20%) can be attempted as early as weeks 5-12, based on urine output monitoring. The primary endpoint in the STEPS trial was at 24 weeks, when 63% of teduglutide patients achieved at least 20% reduction in weekly PS volume vs 30% on placebo. Complete TPN independence was achieved in some patients in long-term extensions.

faqs.q: Is teduglutide safe with kidney disease?
faqs.a: The FDA label requires a 50% dose reduction (to 0.025 mg/kg/day) for moderate-to-severe renal impairment (eGFR under 60) or end-stage renal disease. A dedicated PK study showed 2.1x higher peak levels and 2.6x higher total exposure in ESRD patients. That's a dose adjustment, not a contraindication.

faqs.q: What cancer screening is required during teduglutide treatment?
faqs.a: Colonoscopy must be done within 6 months before starting. Repeat at 1 year post-initiation, then at least every 5 years. Any colorectal polyps must be removed before you begin. If malignancy is found, stop teduglutide. The requirement exists because the drug's trophic effects on gut tissue could theoretically accelerate neoplastic growth.

faqs.q: Does teduglutide have off-label use in fitness or gut healing?
faqs.a: No. While GLP-2 is gut-trophic and the STEPS trial showed lean mass increases, those reflect correction of SBS malabsorption, not muscle-building. The prohibitive cost and mandatory colonoscopy surveillance have prevented any grey-market adoption. BPC-157 fills the "gut healing peptide" niche in performance communities instead.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of Teduglutide (Gattex/Revestive)?
faqs.a: The half-life of Teduglutide (Gattex/Revestive) is ~2 hours (1.3h in SBS patients; range 0.9-3h depending on body weight). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: Sixty-three percent of patients cut their IV nutrition by at least a fifth in 24 weeks. Teduglutide (Gattex in the US, Revestive in Europe) is an FDA-approved GLP-2 receptor agonist that rebuilds the intestinal lining from the inside out, increasing villus height, crypt depth, and absorptive surface area in patients with short bowel syndrome.
